Vignette:
# Karim's Story

Karim was twenty-three when it happened—a night that began as routine and fractured into something he has spent four years trying to forget, even as his body refuses to let him. He had gone to a nightclub in downtown Boston with colleagues from the rehabilitation clinic where he was doing his clinical internship. The air was thick with cologne and perfume, the kind of sensory saturation he usually found energizing. He remembered the bass thrumming through his chest, the press of bodies on the dance floor, the sense of being young and invulnerable. He remembered a man—someone he thought was friendly, someone who had bought him drinks—guiding him toward a back hallway. He remembered the smell of that man's cologne, something with amber and musk, and then the shock of being shoved into a bathroom stall, the sudden violence of it, hands that were not his own on his body, pain that seemed to split him in half.

When Karim left the bathroom, he told no one. He drove home in silence, showered until his skin was raw, and went to bed as if nothing had happened. For weeks he functioned—he completed his internship, graduated with his DPT, married Yasmin, whom he had been dating since college. But the world had become a place of hidden threats. Certain scents—cologne, perfume, even some of the stronger essential oils his clinic used in the wellness room—would send him into a state of alert so acute that his hands would shake. He found himself unable to be touched unexpectedly. When Yasmin reached for him in the kitchen, or when a patient at the clinic accidentally brushed against him during a treatment, he would flinch violently, his nervous system hijacking his response before his mind could catch up.

The pain in his body—a chronic tension in his lower back and hips, the very places where he had been hurt—became a constant sentinel. He began checking himself obsessively, pressing on his ribs and abdomen, assessing his own body as though it might betray him again. At work, where he spent his days helping patients recover from their own injuries, he would find himself dissociating during certain moments. When a male patient came in after being assaulted, or when he had to touch someone's lower back, he would mentally step outside himself, imagining that it was someone else in the room, someone else's hands moving across the patient's spine. This dissociation was a relief, a way of making the work survivable.

What had begun as avoidance of specific triggers—he started declining social invitations, making excuses not to go to restaurants or shops where he might encounter strong scents—had calcified into something larger. Intimacy with Yasmin became impossible. She would initiate sex and he would feel panic rising in his throat, his body rigid, his mind somewhere else entirely. He had come to believe that he would never feel normal again, that something fundamental had been broken in him. The shame was suffocating—shame not just about what had been done to him, but about his body itself, as though it had somehow invited this violation. He had come to distrust his own judgment, his own ability to keep himself safe. If he could be hurt in a place full of people, if his instincts had failed him so completely, how could he trust anything his mind told him?

By twenty-seven, Karim's life had contracted around these fears. He had stopped going to the clinic's social events. He avoided certain streets where the nightclub was located. He had begun wearing noise-canceling headphones even at home, a barrier between himself and the world. Yasmin had grown distant, hurt and confused by his withdrawal. Last month, after she asked him directly whether he was still attracted to her, and he could not answer because the truth was too complicated and too shameful, she suggested that he speak to someone. It was not an ultimatum, but it felt close. Karim finally called a trauma-informed therapist, terrified of what it would mean to put the event into words, but more terrified still of losing the one person who had stayed.
